title: A seat at the king's table (2 Samuel 9)
hook: David looks for any of Saul's family to show kindness, and finds a lame grandson

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king in a plain linen ephod, dancing before the ark. Your line was with all his might.

"Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" That's the king's question. From a new king, a question about the old king's family could sound like a threat. They find a servant of Saul's house named Ziba, and he answers. There is one: a son of Jonathan, living in a place called Lo-debar, in another man's house. And Ziba adds one more detail, as if it might matter to the king: he is lame on his feet.
screen: `ANY LEFT OF THE HOUSE OF SAUL?`

segments.voice: His name is Mephibosheth. Earlier in the book we learn how he became lame: when he was five, news came that Saul and Jonathan had died, and his nurse snatched him up to flee, and in her hurry he fell. Now he's grown, with a young son of his own, the grandson of the fallen king, and he's summoned to the palace. He falls on his face before David, and David's first words are: "Fear not." Then the promise, in the King James Bible: "I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually." Kindness, in Hebrew, is chesed: loyal love, the faithfulness that keeps a promise. David and Jonathan had sworn that their love would reach their children. Jonathan is gone. David keeps it anyway. Mephibosheth can hardly take it in: "What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?" That's how small he feels. And the chapter's last line puts two facts side by side, with no comment: he "did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet." He is still lame. He still eats at the king's table. The kindness doesn't erase his story; it gives it a place. Some Christians hear their own story here: brought in from far away, given a seat they didn't earn, for someone else's sake, a picture of grace. Others simply hear a king keeping a promise to a dead friend.
screen: `SUCH A DEAD DOG AS I AM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've been at odds with, then look past them to the people around them: a child, a parent, a friend who had nothing to do with your quarrel. Choose one, and picture what kindness to them would look like: a greeting, a small help, including them instead of avoiding them. If you pray, hold that person before God by name.
Mephibosheth. Jonathan's lame son, Saul's grandson, brought in by David and given a seat at the king's table as a promise of loyal love.
Your line: always at my table. A promise to a friend, kept for his son. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians tell the story of Mephibosheth as a picture of grace and of keeping promises, and preachers use it to speak about welcoming people who have been left out.
